title: Australian Passport Photo Mistakes: Examples and Fixes
metaTitle: Australian Passport Photo Rejected? 26 Mistakes and Fixes
metaDescription: Why Australian passport photos are rejected: 26 unacceptable examples from the official guidelines, grouped, with a simple fix for each one.
excerpt: Every unacceptable example from the Australian Passport Office guidelines, grouped by face, lighting, accessories and print, with why each fails and how to fix it.
keyTakeaways: The official guidelines list 26 kinds of unacceptable photo.
Common ones: smiling, shadows, glasses, a tilted head, hair over the eyes and a background that is not plain.
Print faults count too: lines, streaks, ink marks, blur and grain.
Retouching is never allowed, so fix problems by retaking, not editing.
intro: **Quick answer:** The most common problems in Australian passport photos are smiling, shadows, glasses, a tilted head, hair over the eyes and a background that is not plain. Print faults, such as streaks or ink marks, also count. Fix the problem by retaking the photo, not by editing it, then check it again.
**[Check my photo with the Australian passport photo checker →](/australian-passport-photo-checker)**

Below, every unacceptable example from the official guidelines is grouped by type, with why it fails and how to fix it. For the full rule list, see the [Australian passport photo requirements](/guides/australian-passport-photo-requirements).

sections.heading: What does an acceptable Australian passport photo look like?

subsections.heading: The checklist at a glance
content:
- 2 colour prints, 35-40 mm wide x 45-50 mm high
- head 32-36 mm from chin to crown
- less than 6 months old
- plain white or light grey background
- even lighting, no shadows or reflections
- face centred and straight on, eyes open, neutral expression (over 3)
- edges of the face visible, hair off the face
- dye-sublimation print on glossy paper of at least 200 gsm
- no retouching

subsections.heading: Acceptable vs unacceptable examples
content: The official guidelines show an acceptable photo next to many unacceptable ones. An acceptable photo is sharp, evenly lit and plain, with the person looking straight at the camera.
The unacceptable examples each show one fault. We have grouped all 26 below.

subsections.heading: Why the details matter
content: Your photo needs to show your face clearly and accurately so it can be compared with you. Small faults, such as a slight head tilt or a shadow, can make that harder.
That is why the guidelines are strict about lighting, pose and print quality.

sections.heading: What face and pose mistakes cause problems?

subsections.heading: Smiling or a subtle expression
content: **Problem:** Smiling, or a slight expression such as raised eyebrows or a half smile.
**Why it fails:** People over 3 need a neutral expression. Smiling and a subtle expression are both listed as unacceptable.
**Fix:** Relax your face, close your mouth and look straight at the camera.

subsections.heading: Head tilted, turned or looking away
content: **Problem:** Head tilted up or down, turned to the side, or eyes looking away from the camera.
**Why it fails:** Each of these is listed as unacceptable. Your face must be centred and straight on.
**Fix:** Keep your chin level, square your shoulders and look into the lens.

subsections.heading: Hair covering the eyes or face partly covered
content: **Problem:** Hair over the eyes, or part of the face hidden by hair, clothing or a hand.
**Why it fails:** Hair covering the eyes and a partly covered face are both listed. The edges of your face must be visible.
**Fix:** Tie hair back or tuck it behind your ears, and keep everything away from your face.

sections.heading: What lighting and background mistakes cause problems?

subsections.heading: Shadows, uneven lighting and red eye
content: **Problem:** Shadows on the face or background, one side brighter than the other, or red eyes.
**Why it fails:** Uneven lighting and red eye are both listed as unacceptable.
**Fix:** Face a soft, even light source and avoid direct flash. Retake instead of editing out red eye.

subsections.heading: A background that is not plain, or is edited
content: **Problem:** A patterned wall, objects behind you, or a background that has been removed or replaced.
**Why it fails:** The background must be plain white or light grey. A background that is not plain or has been edited is listed as unacceptable.
**Fix:** Stand in front of a real plain white or light grey wall or screen.

subsections.heading: Camera too close, or framing too close or too far
content: **Problem:** A face that looks stretched, or a head that is too big or too small in the frame.
**Why it fails:** Distortion from a camera that is too close, framing too close and framing too far are all listed. The head must be 32-36 mm from chin to crown.
**Fix:** Have someone else take the photo from further away, then crop it to the right head size. See our [size guide](/guides/australian-passport-photo-size).

sections.heading: What accessory and clothing mistakes cause problems?

subsections.heading: Glasses, hats and patterned head coverings
content: **Problem:** Wearing glasses or a hat, or a religious head covering with a pattern.
**Why it fails:** Glasses are not allowed unless they cannot be removed for medical reasons. Hats are listed as unacceptable, and religious head coverings must be plain.
**Fix:** Remove glasses and hats. Wear a plain head covering that shows your whole face from chin to forehead.

subsections.heading: Wireless earbuds and too much make-up
content: **Problem:** AirPods or other wireless earbuds in your ears, or heavy make-up.
**Why it fails:** Earbuds are not hearing aids and must be removed. Too much make-up is listed as unacceptable.
**Fix:** Take earbuds out (hearing aids can stay in) and keep make-up light and natural.

subsections.heading: Objects in the photo (for babies: toys and hands)
content: **Problem:** A toy, a dummy or a parent's hand in a baby's photo.
**Why it fails:** An object in the photo and a parent's hand in the photo are both listed. No one else can be visible.
**Fix:** Keep toys behind the camera and hands out of the frame. See our [baby photo guide](/guides/australian-baby-passport-photo).

sections.heading: What print and image quality mistakes cause problems?

subsections.heading: Lines, streaks and ink marks
content: **Problem:** Lines or streaks across the photo, or ink marks on the print.
**Why it fails:** These come from printing or scanning, and are listed as unacceptable. Inkjet prints are not accepted.
**Fix:** Get dye-sublimation prints from a professional provider and keep them clean and flat.

subsections.heading: Blurred, grainy or reduced-resolution images
content: **Problem:** A soft or blurry face, visible grain or noise, or a photo that looks pixelated.
**Why it fails:** Blur, grain and reduced resolution are all listed as unacceptable.
**Fix:** Use good light, hold the camera steady, and print from the original full-quality file.

subsections.heading: Retouching and skin smoothing
content: **Problem:** Skin smoothing, beauty filters, or removing moles, wrinkles or scars.
**Why it fails:** Retouching is not allowed, because the photo must show how you really look.
**Fix:** Turn off beauty modes and ask your provider not to retouch the photo.

sections.heading: What happens if your photo is not accepted?

subsections.heading: You may be asked for new photos
content: If your photos do not meet the guidelines, you may be asked for new ones, either when you lodge your application or later while it is being assessed.
That can delay your passport.

subsections.heading: How to fix and retake
content: Find the fault in the groups above, fix it and take a new photo. Do not edit the old one, because retouching is not allowed.
If a provider took the photo, explain the problem and ask for a retake.

subsections.heading: Check it before you apply
content: Our [Australian passport photo checker](/australian-passport-photo-checker) flags common problems such as head height, background, lighting and glasses.
It cannot check print quality or paper, and a pass is not an approval, but it catches many of the faults above.

faq.question: Why was my Australian passport photo rejected?
faq.answer: The most common reasons are a smile or expression, glasses, shadows or uneven lighting, a tilted head, hair over the eyes, a background that is not plain, the wrong head size, or print faults like streaks and ink marks. Compare your photo with the groups on this page to find the fault.

faq.question: Can I wear make-up in my Australian passport photo?
faq.answer: Yes, but keep it light. Too much make-up is one of the official examples of an unacceptable photo. Your photo must show how you normally look, so avoid heavy contouring, shimmer or anything that changes the shape of your face or causes reflections.

faq.question: Can I wear wireless earbuds in my passport photo?
faq.answer: No. AirPods and other wireless earbuds are not hearing aids, and they are listed as unacceptable. Take them out before the photo is taken. Hearing aids are different: adults, children and babies can wear hearing aids in an Australian passport photo.

faq.question: Can I use a filter or edit my passport photo?
faq.answer: No. Retouching is not allowed, including skin smoothing, removing moles, wrinkles or scars, and editing the background. Turn off beauty modes and filters on the camera. If your photo has a problem, take a new one instead of trying to fix it with editing.

faq.question: How can I check my photo before applying?
faq.answer: Compare it with the official guidelines and the checklist on this page. You can also upload it to our Australian passport photo checker, which flags head height, background, lighting and glasses problems. A pass is a helpful guide, but it is not an approval from the Passport Office.
